q4_convergence.criterion: median of four best-run minimum training losses
q4_convergence.interpretation: Using the common threshold 6.909404, ADAMW reached it in the fewest optimization steps, while RMSPROP reached it in the least synchronized training time. The rankings differ. Measured mean seconds/step from fastest to slowest were: sgd=0.0727s, rmsprop=0.0732s, adamw=0.0857s, muon=0.1154s. This measured per-step cost explains why an optimizer can require fewer steps yet not be the fastest in wall-clock time.

q4_lr_sensitivity.conclusion: Learning-rate sensitivity is assessed from the equal 100-step screening sweeps, so every point within an optimizer has the same training budget. Tested screening LRs were: sgd=0.001,0.005,0.02,0.08; rmsprop=3e-05,0.0001,0.0005,0.001; adamw=3e-05,0.0001,0.0003,0.001; muon=0.002,0.005,0.02,0.05. The largest measured worst/best held-out-PPL ratio was SGD (34155438145593680125682991375736399203826353900966167315537921329594368.000x). SGD was more sensitive than the most sensitive adaptive optimizer (ADAMW): 34155438145593680125682991375736399203826353900966167315537921329594368.000x versus 7443639417.406x. This conclusion is based on the recorded HPO results rather than an assumed optimizer ranking.

q4_muon_split_ablation.interpretation: With the same LR (0.02), initialization, data order, and 500-step budget, recommended Muon+AdamW obtained held-out PPL 8752.6433 and the broad Muon-style variant obtained 1197.0014 (broad minus recommended = -7555.6419, -86.32%). The mean of the last 50 training losses was 9.1949 vs 6.8817. Using a transparent 5% relative-PPL heuristic for a noticeable effect at this scale, the difference is meaningful; the broad Muon-style split is better.
